Ownership and Borrowing

Stack and heaps


fn main() {
    let s = String::from("Hello");
}
s is a pointer, length and capacity on the stack; the five bytes live on the heap. s owns that allocation, and the heap memory is freed when s goes out of scope at the closing brace. Assigning let t = s; moves ownership, after which s can no longer be used.
borrow mutable ONCE: at any point, a value has either one &mut reference or any number of & references, never both. The compiler checks this at compile time, which rules out data races on that value. See the book, ch. 4.

long running owners
refcount: when ownership has to be shared, Rc<T> counts owners in one thread and Arc<T> uses atomic counts across threads. The value is dropped when the count reaches zero. A cycle of Rcs never reaches zero; Weak breaks it.

Foreign-Function Interfaces (FFI)
Declare foreign functions in an extern "C" block and call them inside unsafe, since the compiler cannot check the other side’s ownership rules. Structs passed across the boundary need #[repr(C)] to get C layout. See the Rustonomicon on FFI.
